title: Hadamard Maximal Determinant
origin: In 1893, Jacques Hadamard posed an interesting question: given an n x n matrix whose entries are all +1 or -1, what is the largest possible value of its determinant? It took over a century of effort for finding exact answers for some small matrices (n up to 22). For n = 23 and beyond, much less is known. The best values found so far come from computer searches by Orrick, Solomon, Dowdeswell, and Smith in 2003, using hill-climbing and simulated annealing. Most of those records have stood unchallenged for over 20 years.
instance: For any value of n from the records table below, construct an n x n matrix (M) consisting of only +1 and -1 such that the absolute value of the determinant (|det(M)|) is strictly larger than the current known maximum value for that particular n. For example, the record for n = 23 is |det(M)| = 2,779,447,296,000,000. To claim a new record, submit a single matrix that beats this value. Each n is an independent challenge and you only need to improve one.

scoring.summary: Each submission is scored on how close its determinant gets to the theoretical upper bound for the chosen n.

metrics.name: Bound ratio
metrics.description: The primary score is |det(M)| / B(n), where B(n) is the theoretical upper bound (Hadamard, Barba, Ehlich-Wojtas, or Ehlich depending on n mod 4). This gives a percentage between 0% and 100%. Higher is better.

metrics.name: New record
metrics.description: If |det(M)| strictly exceeds the previously best known value for that n, the submission is flagged as a new record and the submitter is credited on the leaderboard.

metrics.name: Tiebreaker
metrics.description: If two submissions achieve the same determinant for the same n, the earlier submission ranks higher.

scoring.note: Submissions that match but do not beat the current record are still accepted and scored. Getting to 93% of the theoretical bound is meaningful even without setting a new record.

verification: We compute the exact integer determinant of your matrix using sympy (no floating point). The submission is accepted if the matrix is n x n, all entries are +1 or -1, and |det(M)| matches your claimed_det. It scores if |det(M)| is at or above the current record for that n.

bounds.label: n mod 4 ≡ 0
bounds.name: Hadamard bound
bounds.formula: n^(n/2). Tight when a Hadamard matrix exists.

bounds.label: n mod 4 ≡ 3
bounds.name: Ehlich bound
bounds.formula: Derived from eigenvalue analysis of M^T M. See Ehlich (1964).

witnessExample.note: Record-holding matrix for n = 23 from Orrick et al. (2003). Determinant = 2,779,447,296,000,000 (93.2% of theoretical bound). Use this to verify your search is producing competitive results.

leaderboard.note: Best known determinants from Orrick et al. (2003), arXiv:math/0304410. All values are raw (not normalized).

suggestedApproach.title: Pick an n
suggestedApproach.body: Any row in the records table. n = 23 is the smallest open case and has the most literature. n = 27 has no known factored form, which is unusual.

suggestedApproach.title: Random start
suggestedApproach.body: Generate a random {+1, -1} matrix. Compute its determinant.

suggestedApproach.title: Hill-climb
suggestedApproach.body: Flip entries that increase |det|. Cofactor expansion lets you update the determinant cheaply (O(n^2) per flip) without recomputing from scratch.

suggestedApproach.title: Simulated annealing
suggestedApproach.body: Accept some determinant-decreasing flips to escape local maxima. This is exactly how the Orrick et al. 2003 records were set.

agentPrompt: I want you to find a {+1, -1} matrix of size n = 23 whose determinant (in absolute value) exceeds 2,779,447,296,000,000 (the current record, factored as 2^22 x 3 x 5^6 x 67 x 211). Use hill-climbing with simulated annealing: start from a random +/-1 matrix, repeatedly flip entries that increase |det(M)| using cofactor updates, and randomly perturb when stuck in a local maximum. Run many restarts and report the best matrix found. Output the matrix as a JSON array of arrays, and report the determinant value.
